summary: Defines a metric for one-way packet loss across Internet paths. It builds on the IPPM framework in RFC 2330 and makes RFC 2680 obsolete.

eli5.summary: This says how to count how many packets vanish on the trip from here to there.

subtitle: How to define and report whether a single test packet made it across an Internet path, and how often.

tldr.problem: Operators and researchers need a precise, comparable way to say how many packets are lost in one direction between two hosts, because round-trip numbers mix two different paths together.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a single-packet metric that is 0 for received and 1 for lost, a sample of those values taken at Poisson-distributed times, and a loss ratio computed as the average of the sample.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that makes RFC 2680 obsolete, and it gives IPPM measurements a common vocabulary for loss and for what must be reported alongside it.

facts.value: Src, Dst, T0, Tf, Tmax, lambda

today: RFC 7680 is an Internet Standard (STD 82) and obsoletes RFC 2680; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Metric Built in Three Steps
sections.content:
RFC 7680 defines a metric for one-way packet loss across Internet paths. It builds on the IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) framework in RFC 2330 and assumes the reader knows that document and its update, RFC 7312. It is written to parallel the companion one-way delay metric in RFC 7679.

The document moves in three steps and insists on keeping them separate. First a singleton, called Type-P-One-way-Packet-Loss, records one packet's fate. Then a sample, Type-P-One-way-Packet-Loss-Poisson-Stream, collects many singletons taken at times drawn from a Poisson process. Finally statistics such as a loss ratio summarise the sample.

The RFC 2119 key words are used here to make results from two different implementations comparable and to flag cases where an implementation could disturb the network.
sections.eli5: First you check one paper plane, then you throw a whole bunch at random moments, then you work out what fraction got lost. Each step stays separate so nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: Why Measure Loss in One Direction
sections.content:
Loss matters because some applications do not perform well, or at all, when end-to-end loss between hosts is large relative to some threshold. Excessive loss can make real-time applications hard to support, and the larger the loss, the harder it is for transport protocols to sustain high bandwidths.

The RFC prefers one-way over round-trip measurement for several reasons. The forward and reverse paths may differ (asymmetric paths), so a round trip measures two distinct paths at once. Even symmetric paths can behave differently because of asymmetric queuing. An application, such as a TCP transfer, may depend mostly on one direction, and where quality of service is enabled the provisioning in each direction may differ.

The RFC says it is outside its scope to say precisely how loss metrics would be applied to specific problems.
sections.eli5: If a letter goes to your friend by one road and the reply comes back by another, counting only the round trip hides which road lost the mail. Counting each direction separately shows where the trouble is.

sections.title: The Singleton: Lost or Not
sections.content:
The singleton metric takes four parameters: Src and Dst (IP addresses of two hosts), T (a time) and Tmax (a loss threshold waiting time). Its value is 0 if Src sent the first bit of a Type-P packet at wire time T and Dst received it, and 1 if Dst did not receive it within Tmax.

The RFC ties this to the delay metric: loss is 0 exactly when one-way delay is a finite value, and 1 exactly when delay is undefined. It then settles awkward cases. A packet that arrives corrupted counts as lost. A packet duplicated so that several non-corrupt copies arrive counts as received. A fragmented packet that is not reassembled counts as lost.

Times in the document are measured in seconds and fractions relative to UTC. The RFC also distinguishes four clock notions taken from the framework: synchronization, accuracy, resolution and skew.
sections.eli5: Each packet gets a score: 0 if it arrived in time, 1 if it did not. A smashed or half-delivered packet counts as not arrived, but if two copies show up, it still counts as arrived.

sections.title: Measuring, Errors and Reporting
sections.content:
A generic methodology is sketched: synchronize the clocks at Src and Dst, build a test packet of the chosen Type-P, put a timestamp in it and send it, and note whether it arrives within a reasonable time. If it does not arrive within Tmax, the loss is 1. The RFC leaves the packet format and how the hosts agree on timing outside its scope.

Three sources of error are named: clock synchronization between the hosts, the loss threshold (which is related to synchronization), and resource limits in the receiving instrument's interface or software. A threshold set too low can make many packets look lost, and an overloaded instrument can drop a packet the network actually delivered.

Results MUST be reported together with their context. The exact Type-P used, the threshold Tmax and the degree of synchronization between the clocks MUST be reported, and the path traversed SHOULD be reported if possible. The RFC notes that recording the exact path is often impractical.
sections.eli5: To be fair, both people need clocks that agree, and you must decide how long to wait before calling a plane lost. When you share your results, you also tell everyone what kind of plane you threw and how long you waited.

sections.title: Samples Taken at Poisson Times
sections.content:
A sample fixes Src, Dst and Type-P and then chooses many values of T. The parameters are a start time T0, an end time Tf, Tmax and an average rate lambda in reciprocal seconds. The times come from a pseudorandom Poisson process of rate lambda, so the interval between successive times averages 1/lambda. The sample is the sequence of time and loss pairs, and it is empty if there are none.

Poisson sampling is used to avoid self-synchronization effects and to limit bias. The RFC says it is only one way to sample: a truncated Poisson distribution may be needed to avoid reactive network state changes, and RFC 3432 describes periodic sampling with random start times.

The RFC does not constrain lambda except to note the extremes. A rate that is too large perturbs the network and itself causes congestion, while one that is too small may miss interesting behavior. Care must also be taken with out-of-order arrival, and reordering metrics are found in RFC 4737.
sections.eli5: Instead of throwing planes on a regular beat, you throw them at random moments so nobody can game the rhythm. Throw too many and you clog the room; throw too few and you miss what is happening.

sections.title: The Packet Loss Ratio
sections.content:
The main statistic is Type-P-One-way-Packet-Loss-Ratio: the average of all the L values in the stream, that is, losses divided by total packets. It is undefined if the sample is empty. In the RFC's example of five singletons with one loss, the result is 0.2.

The RFC points out a practical difficulty. Healthy Internet paths should operate at loss ratios below 1%, so telling apart fractions of 1% over one-minute periods may need several hundred samples per minute, which means a larger lambda than one would ordinarily want. If the chance that an arrived packet is counted as lost because of resource exhaustion is significant compared to the loss ratio of interest, the ratio is meaningless.
sections.eli5: If you threw five planes and one never arrived, one out of five got lost, which is 0.2. When almost nothing is lost, you need to throw a lot of planes to see tiny differences.

sections.title: Security and Privacy of Measurements
sections.content:
The memo does not specify an implementation, so it does not directly affect Internet security. It names two kinds of concern: harm caused by the measurements and harm to the measurements.

Because the measurements are active, they inject packets, and parameters MUST be chosen so that they inject trivial amounts of traffic. Too much traffic skews results and in extreme cases causes congestion and denial of service. Measurements can be harmed if routers treat measurement traffic differently from normal traffic, or if an attacker injects artificial traffic, which would artificially lower the loss ratio. Methodologies SHOULD therefore make measurement traffic hard to distinguish from normal traffic, and authentication such as digital signatures may be used against injection.

For privacy, active techniques reduce the sensitive information available to observers, while passive observation of user traffic raises many privacy issues. Access to results or control of measurement systems should be guarded against use for reconnaissance.
sections.eli5: Your test planes should not fill up the room, and nobody should be able to sneak extra planes in to make things look better than they are. Keep the results private too, so no one uses them to plan mischief.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2680
sections.content:
RFC 7680 revises RFC 2680, which is now an Internet Standard. The test plan and results supporting that advancement are in RFC 7290, whose conclusions list four minor modifications. Among them, post-processing to enforce a constant waiting time threshold is declared compliant, and the Packet Loss Average statistic is renamed the Packet Loss Ratio. References to RFC 6703 on reporting were added, and two errata were incorporated.

Further updates reference key IPPM RFCs approved after RFC 2680. They include explicit inclusion of the maximum waiting time parameter, replacing the term "precedence" with DS Field, a reference to RFC 3432 on periodic sampling, recognition of time-slotted links from RFC 7312, a reference to RFC 4737 on reordering, and expanded privacy and reconnaissance material in the security section.
sections.eli5: This is the same game with clearer rules. The writers fixed small mistakes, gave one number a better name, and added newer advice.
